title: Open-weight vs closed AI models in 2026: which should startups use?
excerpt: DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral and Llama vs OpenAI, Anthropic and Google: licences, token prices, GPU costs and data privacy compared for founders in 2026.
content:
Most startups should build their first product on a closed API (OpenAI, Anthropic or Google), then move high-volume or sensitive workloads to an open-weight model such as DeepSeek V4.1, Qwen3.8, Mistral Small 4 or gpt-oss once usage is predictable. Open weights now come close to closed models on price and capability. The real differences are in licence terms, data control and how much infrastructure work you're willing to take on. This guide compares both routes as of 6 October 2026, using the vendors' own licence and pricing pages.

The question is timely because the open-weight field shifted this year. DeepSeek released V4.1-Flash under the MIT licence on 10 September. Meta made its flagship Muse Spark proprietary in April, then released an open model, Muse Glimmer, in August. And the biggest new Qwen and Mistral models no longer come with plain open licences.

Key takeaways

  • "Open" no longer means one thing. DeepSeek (MIT), gpt-oss, Gemma 4, Muse Glimmer and Mistral Small 4 (Apache 2.0) are permissive. Mistral Medium 3.5 bars companies earning over $20 million a month, and Llama 4 has a 700-million-user cap and EU limits on multimodal use.
  • Hosted open models are cheap. DeepSeek V4.1-Flash costs $0.30 in and $1.20 out per million tokens at peak on DeepSeek's own API, against $2 and $10 for OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol.
  • Self-hosting pays only at scale. One dedicated H100 GPU on Together AI costs $5.49 an hour, or about $3,950 for a month running non-stop.
  • Privacy is a hosting choice. The big closed APIs don't train on paid API data by default. DeepSeek's own app and API store data in China, but its MIT-licensed weights can run on servers you choose.

Open-weight, open source and closed: what the labels mean

A closed model (GPT-6, Claude, Gemini) is only reachable through its maker's API or apps. You never see the weights, and the vendor decides prices, rate limits and when old versions retire. An open-weight model publishes its trained weights for download, so you can run it on your own servers, fine-tune it and ship it inside your product. "Open source" in the strict sense also implies an approved licence with no use restrictions. Most open-weight models don't release their training data, and several use custom licences that add conditions.

For a startup, the practical test is simple. Read the licence file in the model repository before you build on it, and check it again when you upgrade, because terms can change between versions from the same lab.

The fine print that catches startups

Mistral Medium 3.5. The licence file says you may not exercise any rights if your company's (or your employer's) global consolidated monthly revenue exceeded $20 million the previous month. The restriction carries over to derivatives and fine-tunes. Above that line you need a commercial licence from Mistral or its hosted service. Most seed and Series A startups sit well below it, but an enterprise customer may not, so check before you ship it into a client's environment.

Llama 4. Meta's community licence requires a separate licence once your products pass 700 million monthly active users. It also asks you to display "Built with Llama" and to start the name of any derived model with "Llama". Its acceptable use policy withholds the multimodal licence from individuals domiciled in the EU and from companies headquartered there, though end users of products built on the models aren't affected. That matters to Indian startups with a European entity.

Meta's direction. Meta debuted Muse Spark on 8 April, and Mark Zuckerberg said it plans to release new open source models too, according to TechCrunch. In August it released Muse Glimmer, a 30-billion-parameter model with Apache 2.0 weights designed to run agents on consumer hardware, TechCrunch reported. Llama 4 remains available, but the newest Llama checkpoints on Meta's Hugging Face page date from April 2025.

Cost: API pricing versus hosting your own

Here's what one million tokens costs on standard, pay-as-you-go pricing as of 6 October 2026.

Gemini 3.8 Flash$0.75 / $3.75 (doubles 1 January 2027)Gemini API

Sources: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek and Together AI. DeepSeek's peak hours are 01:00–04:00 and 06:00–10:00 UTC on weekdays. Both OpenAI and Anthropic offer 50% off for batch jobs.

Self-hosting changes the maths from per-token to per-hour. Together AI lists a dedicated NVIDIA HGX H100 at $5.49 per GPU-hour and a B200 at $8.99. By our arithmetic, one H100 running for 30 days costs about $3,950. The same money buys roughly 3.3 billion output tokens of DeepSeek V4.1-Flash on Together's serverless API, or about 395 million output tokens of GPT-6.1 Sol. A dedicated GPU only wins if you keep it busy around the clock, or if you need the isolation more than the savings.

Size matters too. OpenAI says gpt-oss-120b fits on a single 80GB GPU, according to its model card, and Muse Glimmer's model card describes quantised builds for 24GB to 32GB graphics cards. DeepSeek's 552-billion-parameter V4.1-Flash needs a multi-GPU server, which is why most teams use it through an API.

Control, customisation and lock-in

Open weights give you three things an API can't. You can freeze a version, so a model update never silently changes your product's behaviour. You can fine-tune deeply on your own data, including full-weight training rather than the limited tuning some APIs offer. And you can switch hosts: the same DeepSeek or Qwen weights run on DeepSeek, Together, your own cloud account or an on-premise server.

Closed APIs win on everything around the model. You get frontier capability, tool use, long context, safety filters and uptime without hiring an inference team. Prices also keep falling: OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna, at $0.10 in and $0.50 out per million tokens, is cheaper than gpt-oss-120b on Together AI. For a five-person team, the engineering hours saved usually outweigh the per-token premium.

The sensible middle path is to write your app against an abstraction layer that speaks the common chat-completions format. Many open-model hosts accept it, so swapping a closed model for an open one is a configuration change rather than a rewrite.

Data privacy and where your data goes

All three big closed APIs say they don't train on paid API traffic by default. OpenAI says API data isn't used to train its models unless you opt in, and keeps abuse-monitoring logs for up to 30 days, according to its data controls guide. Zero Data Retention needs OpenAI's approval. OpenAI also lists India as a data residency region, but it covers storage only, not processing, and requires extra approval. Anthropic says it won't use inputs or outputs from its commercial products, including the API, for training by default, unless you submit feedback or opt in, according to its privacy centre. Google's Gemini API pricing page says free-tier content is used to improve its products and paid-tier content isn't. Don't send customer data through a free key.

Open weights put the decision in your hands. DeepSeek's privacy policy, updated 10 February 2026, says it collects, processes and stores personal data in the People's Republic of China. That applies to its own app and API, not to the weights. Run DeepSeek V4.1-Flash on a server in Mumbai or Hyderabad and your prompts never reach DeepSeek. India also offers a public option. The government's Bhashini platform now hosts open-sourced Sarvam models on what it calls a sovereign cloud, according to a PIB release of 12 March 2026.

This is general information, not legal advice. For obligations under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act or the EU's GDPR, confirm with a qualified lawyer.

A decision framework for founders

  • Pre-product-market fit: use a closed API. Speed of iteration matters more than cost, and frontier models hide prompt weaknesses.
  • High-volume, simple tasks (classification, extraction, routing): test a hosted open model such as gpt-oss-120b or DeepSeek V4.1-Flash. Output costs can be a fraction of frontier-model rates.
  • Regulated or sensitive data (health, finance, government): self-host an Apache 2.0 or MIT model in your own cloud region, or use a closed API with a signed zero-retention agreement.
  • Indian languages: evaluate Sarvam-105B, which says it was trained with a focus on 22 Indian languages, against a frontier API on your own test set.
  • On-device or offline: Muse Glimmer, Gemma 4 or the smaller Qwen3.8 models.
  • Enterprise customers above $20M monthly revenue: avoid Mistral Medium 3.5 unless you or they hold a commercial licence.

Teams with machine-learning engineers can make the move to open weights sooner. If you're hiring for that skill set, or looking for such a role, our AI and ML jobs board lists openings at companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.

Bottom line: Start closed and design for portability. Move to open weights when one of three things happens: your token bill becomes a top-three cost, a customer contract demands that data stay on your infrastructure, or you need a model version that never changes. Whichever way you go, read the licence file, not the press release.

Frequently asked questions

Is DeepSeek safe for an Indian startup to use?

Its own app and API store data in China, according to its privacy policy. The MIT-licensed weights can be self-hosted or used through a third-party host, so your data never reaches DeepSeek.

Can I use Llama 4 commercially?

Yes, under the Llama 4 Community Licence, until your products pass 700 million monthly active users. You must show "Built with Llama". EU-based companies don't get the licence for its multimodal models.

Which open-weight model is cheapest to run?

On Together AI, gpt-oss-120b costs $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens as of 6 October 2026. It also fits on one 80GB GPU if you host it yourself.

Do OpenAI, Anthropic and Google train on my API data?

Not by default on paid API use, according to each company. Google's free Gemini API tier is an exception: free-tier content is used to improve its products.

Is Mistral still open source?

Partly. Mistral Small 4 uses Apache 2.0, but Mistral Medium 3.5 uses a modified MIT licence that bars companies with more than $20 million in monthly revenue.
